doc.title: Chazz Frichtel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 13, 2016

title: Veteran musicians still scrambling; replaced for a younger look
summary: Rowe notes veterans keep seeking gigs; Frichtel recalls being replaced for a younger look and a humbling bar mitzvah after a huge festival.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well I was a bit surprised when I started doing these interviews that some of the veteran musicians, who we may have this, the way we think about them is oh, they have it made, they’ve had their career and they can choose their gigs. Yet those guys were still scrambling. Like “Bring me to your college.” They were constantly seeking the next gig. And, but wait, you played with Basie and you played with Ellington. Yeah, but that was 30 years ago.

I know so many musicians in L.A. that I so look up to. And I know a lot of guys that are scuffling. You know, that are having a tough go. That have resumes that would be the envy of anyone. And a lot of it is just due to the changes in the business and our ages, now as middle-aged people, especially in L.A. which is a pretty youth-oriented place. And it was good for me when I was twenty, thirty, even forty-something. But it was so funny. I never thought of it in those terms until an incident happened where I realized that I was kind of being replaced because they needed a younger person. It wasn’t because I couldn’t do the job, it wasn’t because they didn’t love me, it was because they needed a younger look. And boy that was an ice water over the head moment. Because I just never thought of things in those terms. I thought man if you can play the gig you play the gig. But not always so. All these intangibles. I’ve always said the music business is the one business that thrives on intangibles. You know. It just thrives on intangibles. But I’m lucky, you know, I’ve experienced the music business at almost every level — from the sublime to the ridiculous. I know what it’s like to be treated better than anyone should ever be treated and I know what it’s like to be told to, “Go through the back door, don’t talk to the clients, you’re not going to be fed on the gig” you know, those kind of things. You know in the sweet moments you really relish them because you know that the curve, kind of like the income curve, you know. It’s so funny. One of the things that happened to me was I played a music festival in Charleston, West Virginia with Mike McDonald. I think it was a riverfest. And we were on it and Ray Charles was on it and a bunch of great people. So I think that was a Saturday, we played for like a hundred and twenty thousand people or something like that. So I fly back to L.A. Sunday morning, I’m playing a bar mitzvah Sunday early evening. And we’re playing some bossas and some tunes and I’ve got the tuxedo on in the backyard in Brentwood or someplace. And this kid comes up to me and he goes, “Hey do you guys know any White Snake?” And I said, “No we don’t.” He goes, “You guys suck.” So it was like the night before — so the music business is endlessly humbling.
I’m trying not to laugh. That’s really a good story.
